subject: Geography
description: SW monsoon, NE monsoon, El Nino, onset/withdrawal

questions.stem: The South-West Monsoon normally reaches the southern tip of Kerala around:

options.option_text: 15 April
1 June
1 July
15 August

questions.explanation: The IMD's normal onset date for the SW monsoon at Kerala is 1 June. From there it advances north-east and reaches Delhi by around 29 June and the whole country by 8 July. Withdrawal begins from Rajasthan around 17 September and completes by mid-October. June-September delivers ~75 % of India's total annual rainfall.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Most of Tamil Nadu receives the bulk of its annual rainfall from the:

options.option_text: South-West monsoon
North-East monsoon
Western disturbances
Local convective storms

questions.explanation: The coastal Tamil Nadu belt lies in the rain-shadow of the Western Ghats during the SW monsoon and gets less than half its annual rain during June-September. The North-East monsoon (October-December), also called the retreating monsoon, brings its main rainfall — around 48 % of annual rain. Western disturbances chiefly affect NW India in winter.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The SW monsoon splits into two main branches over the Indian landmass — the Arabian Sea branch and the:

options.option_text: Indian Ocean branch
Bay of Bengal branch
Himalayan branch
Western Ghats branch

questions.explanation: The SW monsoon has two arms. The Arabian Sea branch hits the Western Ghats and gives heavy rain to the west coast (Mumbai ~2,400 mm). The Bay of Bengal branch curves north towards the Himalayan foothills and the NE, drenching Meghalaya's Mawsynram and Cherrapunji (the wettest places on Earth). The two arms merge over northern India around early July.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: An El Niño event typically has what effect on the Indian SW monsoon?

options.option_text: Increases rainfall above normal
Tends to weaken and reduce rainfall
Has no measurable effect
Delays onset but increases total rainfall

questions.explanation: El Niño — warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific — disturbs the Walker circulation and typically weakens the Indian SW monsoon, often causing deficit rainfall. La Niña (the cooler phase) generally favours above-normal Indian monsoon rainfall. The correlation is strong but not perfect — 1997's record-breaking El Niño saw a near-normal monsoon.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The wettest place in India (and currently one of the wettest on Earth) is:

options.option_text: Cherrapunji, Meghalaya
Mawsynram, Meghalaya
Agumbe, Karnataka
Mahabaleshwar, Maharashtra

questions.explanation: Mawsynram in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya receives about 11,870 mm of annual rainfall on average — slightly more than nearby Cherrapunji (Sohra). Both villages receive very heavy rainfall from the Bay of Bengal branch of the SW monsoon, funnelled and lifted by the Khasi Hills. Agumbe and Mahabaleshwar are the wettest spots in South India.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which months make up the South-West monsoon season in India, according to the IMD?

options.option_text: April to July
June to September
July to October
March to August

questions.explanation: IMD's four official seasons: winter (Dec-Feb), pre-monsoon/hot weather (Mar-May), SW monsoon (June-September), post-monsoon / NE monsoon (October-December). About 75 % of India's annual rainfall falls during June-September. The remaining ~10-12 % comes mainly during the NE monsoon over the south-east coast.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The narrow mountain range that blocks the SW monsoon on the west coast and creates a rain-shadow over the Deccan plateau is the:

options.option_text: Eastern Ghats
Western Ghats
Aravalli range
Vindhya range

questions.explanation: The Western Ghats — running ~1,600 km parallel to the west coast — force the Arabian Sea branch of the SW monsoon to rise, cool and rain heavily on the windward side (Mumbai, Mangaluru, Thiruvananthapuram). The leeward Deccan plateau (Pune, Bengaluru, Hyderabad) lies in the rain-shadow and gets much less rainfall. The Eastern Ghats are lower and more broken and do not create a strong rain-shadow effect.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The withdrawal of the South-West monsoon from India follows a fixed sequence. From which region does the retreat begin?

options.option_text: Eastern peninsular coast (Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh)
North-western India (Rajasthan and adjoining Punjab-Haryana)
Central Deccan plateau (Maharashtra and Telangana region)
North-eastern states (Assam, Meghalaya, and Manipur area)

questions.explanation: SW monsoon withdrawal begins from north-western India (Rajasthan, around September 1) and concludes along the Tamil Nadu coast by late December. Many candidates confuse the withdrawal sequence with the onset sequence — onset starts from Kerala (south), but withdrawal starts from Rajasthan (north-west). The NE states, with their high humidity, are among the last to lose the SW monsoon.

questions.stem: The term applied to a temporary weakening or pause in monsoon rainfall over the Indian plains — often triggered when the monsoon trough migrates northward toward the Himalayan foothills — is:

options.option_text: Monsoon depression (a low-pressure system in the Bay of Bengal)
Break monsoon (a period of reduced rainfall over the interior plains)
Cyclonic monsoon (rainfall enhancement by cyclonic circulation)
Retreating monsoon (wind-reversal withdrawal phase from October)

questions.explanation: A 'break monsoon' is a temporary interruption in rainfall over central and peninsular India when the monsoon trough shifts to the Himalayan foothills; rainfall simultaneously intensifies over the sub-Himalayan belt. Option D ('retreating monsoon') is a completely separate phenomenon — it refers to the actual withdrawal of the monsoon system that begins in September, not a mid-season pause.

questions.stem: Which large-scale atmospheric phenomenon describes the intense low-level cross-equatorial jet stream over the western Indian Ocean, named after its discoverer, that supplies the bulk of moisture to the Arabian Sea monsoon branch?

options.option_text: Hadley Circulation (global convective cell between equator and 30°)
Walker Circulation (zonal loop linking the western Pacific warm pool)
Findlater Jet (intense southwesterly current crossing the Somali coast)
Ferrel Cell (mid-latitude indirect circulation between 30° and 60°)

questions.explanation: The Findlater Jet (also called the Somali Jet) is a low-level atmospheric jet at roughly 1.5 km altitude that forms over Somalia and channels intense south-westerly flow into the Arabian Sea, directly fuelling the Arabian Sea branch of the SW monsoon. It was described by J. Findlater in 1969. Walker Circulation (B) is an equatorial zonal loop over the Pacific linked to ENSO — distinct from this specific Arabian Sea moisture conduit.

questions.stem: La Niña conditions in the equatorial Pacific Ocean are generally associated with Indian SW monsoon rainfall that is:

options.option_text: Below-normal, because cooler Pacific SSTs reduce global moisture transport
Above-normal, as enhanced Walker Circulation strengthens cross-equatorial flow
Unchanged, because La Niña has no teleconnection with the Indian monsoon
Below-normal on the coast but above-normal in Madhya Pradesh specifically

questions.explanation: La Niña cools the eastern Pacific and strengthens the Walker Circulation, enhancing convection over the western Pacific and the Indian Ocean. This reinforces the cross-equatorial winds feeding the SW monsoon, typically producing above-normal Indian rainfall. El Niño has the opposite effect. Option C is factually incorrect — the ENSO-monsoon teleconnection is one of the best-documented links in tropical meteorology.

questions.stem: In a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) event, which part of the Indian Ocean records warmer-than-normal sea surface temperatures?

options.option_text: Western Indian Ocean and cooler SSTs in the eastern Indian Ocean near Sumatra
Eastern Indian Ocean near Sumatra and cooler SSTs in the western Indian Ocean
Bay of Bengal with cooler SSTs in the Arabian Sea occurring simultaneously
Arabian Sea only, with no corresponding anomaly in the eastern Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: In a positive IOD, the western Indian Ocean (off the Horn of Africa and Arabian Sea) is anomalously warm while the eastern Indian Ocean (near Sumatra and Indonesia) is cooler. This dipole enhances convection over the western Indian Ocean and strengthens moisture supply to the SW monsoon, favouring above-normal Indian rainfall. Option B describes a negative IOD, which suppresses Indian monsoon and is commonly confused with the positive phase.

questions.stem: The 'onset vortex' — a precursor cyclonic circulation whose formation signals the imminent commencement of the SW monsoon over India — typically develops in the:

options.option_text: Northern Bay of Bengal, driven by land-sea temperature contrast along Odisha
South-eastern Arabian Sea off the Kerala coast, linked to a cyclonic system
Lakshadweep Sea zone, generated by the convergence of the trade winds
Andaman Sea, triggered by deep convection over the Myanmar coastline

questions.explanation: The pre-monsoon 'onset vortex' is a low-level cyclonic circulation that develops in the south-eastern Arabian Sea (roughly off the Kerala–Malabar coast) in late May. Its deepening and intensification is one of the key signals IMD monitors to declare monsoon onset over Kerala. The Andaman Sea does see early monsoon activity (Andaman Islands receive monsoon around May 20), but the classical onset vortex is an Arabian Sea phenomenon, not an Andaman Sea one.

questions.stem: Which index — defined as the standardised sea-level pressure difference between Darwin (Australia) and Tahiti — is used as a classic predictor of Indian SW monsoon strength and was first systematically studied by Sir Gilbert Walker?

options.option_text: Indian Ocean Dipole Index (measuring west-east SST gradient in Indian Ocean)
Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), linked to ENSO strength over the Pacific
Pacific Decadal Oscillation Index (tracking multi-decadal Pacific variability)
Quasi-Biennial Oscillation Index (measuring equatorial stratospheric wind direction)

questions.explanation: The Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) measures the standardised pressure difference between Tahiti and Darwin. A sustained negative SOI indicates El Niño (warm eastern Pacific, weak Indian monsoon); a sustained positive SOI indicates La Niña (cool eastern Pacific, strong monsoon). Gilbert Walker discovered this teleconnection in the early 20th century while studying Indian monsoon failures. The IOD Index (A) is a separate, more recent predictor that focuses on Indian Ocean SST anomalies, not this Pacific pressure seesaw.
